title: COVID-19 Induced Misinformation on YouTube: An Analysis of User Commentary
screen_reason: Reports the share of items in a sample classified as false: a BERT classifier labelled about 21% of ~2.45M YouTube comments and 15% of ~906k replies as 'fake' (claims/speculation verifiably not true). Denominator = all comments/replies on the selected COVID-19 videos, i.e. items that exist, so CONTENT.

estimates.date: Videos posted between 11 March 2020 and 29 July 2021; comments downloaded via the YouTube Data API (16-month observation window)
estimates.measure_type: % of YouTube comments on COVID-19 videos classified as fake (containing claims/speculation verifiably not true)

estimates.page_loc: Results, RQ1 (p. 5); denominators from Table 1 (p. 4); channel ranges restated in Discussion (p. 7)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: BERT (Devlin et al. 2018) supervised classifier trained on 11,771 COVID-19 social-media posts (4,798 labelled misinformation), combining Patwa et al. (2021) posts tagged fake by fact-checking sites (PolitiFact, Snopes, Boomlive) with Serrano et al. (2020) conspiratorial YouTube comments; 90/10 train/test split; overall accuracy 0.91; fake class precision 0.93, recall 0.86, F1 0.89. Authors note the training data predate later pandemic conspiracy theories.
estimates.moderator_quote: We selected videos containing at least one of the keywords mentioned above in their YouTube title or YouTube description. The final list includes 1,565 videos posted by one of the four YouTube channels between the 11th of March 2020 and the 29th of July 2021.
estimates.notes: Corpus is a census of comments on a keyword-selected, single-issue (COVID-19) video set, but the four channels were chosen purposively ('because their pandemic-related videos reached a wide audience on other social media platforms ... and they represent different degrees of partisanship'), hence denom_selection=curated. Per-channel point estimates appear only in Figure 1; the text gives the range: 'Depending on the YouTube channel, we observed that between 16% and 25% of comments contained misinformation' - WHO highest, then CNN, then Fox News, with The Epoch Times lowest. I did not create per-channel rows because no per-channel value is stated. Year coded 2020 as the approximate midpoint of the 11 Mar 2020 - 29 Jul 2021 collection window. QUOTE NOTE: the source text file is a two-column PDF dump in which the two columns are interleaved on every line, so no full sentence is contiguous. The source_quote is the contiguous line fragment carrying both values; the full sentence in the article reads: 'Overall, the classifier categorized about 21% of the comments and 15% of the replies as fake.'

missed_or_uncertain: 1) NOT extracted: the per-channel figures. Only ranges are given in prose ('between 16% and 25% of comments', 'between 13 and 19% of replies'), with the ordering WHO > CNN > Fox News > The Epoch Times; the point values live in Figure 1, which is not reproduced in the text. A range_not_point row would duplicate the two point rows I kept. 2) NOT extracted: the trend statistics - the regression coefficient of 0.004 ('the portion of misinformation increases by a rate of 0.4% per month', Table 5) and 0.005 ('the number of users that post misinformation only has increased by 0.5% each month', Table 6). These are slopes, not shares. The Table 5 intercept (0.172) is the fitted mean per-user proportion of fake comments at the start of the window and is a model-fitted quantity, not a reported share, so I did not keep it. 3) NOT extracted: 'the average ratio of fake replies to fake comments (0.21%) is statistically notably larger than the average ratio of fake replies to legitimate comments (0.13%)' - these are ratios of a reply-level rate conditioned on parent-comment type (and the '%' sign appears to be an error, since the values look like proportions 0.21 and 0.13); not a prevalence share with an interpretable denominator. 4) NOT extracted: engagement means (fake comments 5.753 likes vs legitimate 5.626 likes) - means, not shares. 5) NOT extracted: log-log regression coefficients in Table 7 (WHO 0.994, CNN 0.909, Fox News 0.857, The Epoch Times 1.05). 6) NOT extracted: classifier performance figures (91% accuracy; Serrano et al.'s 89.4%; Das et al.'s 98%) - these are method statistics, and the last two are cited from elsewhere. 7) Country is uncertain: the channels are two US outlets, one US-registered outlet with a global diaspora audience (The Epoch Times) and one intergovernmental body (WHO), and the authors say only that 'our results apply to English-speaking YouTube audiences only'. I coded country_norm=Global; an adjudicator preferring the channel-origin reading could code United States.

rob.design: Non-probability platform corpus with automated classification. Frame: Facebook posts containing YouTube links were queried via the CrowdTangle API using 15 COVID-19 keywords ('pandemic', 'hygiene', 'health', 'lockdown', 'school', 'Fauci', 'covid', 'corona', 'vaccine', 'virus', 'AstraZeneca', 'Pfizer', 'BioNTech', 'Johnson', 'J&J', 'Wuhan'); videos posted after 11 March 2020 by four purposively chosen channels (CNN, Fox News, The Epoch Times, WHO) and containing at least one keyword in the title or description were retained, yielding 1,565 videos (11 Mar 2020 - 29 Jul 2021). All comments and replies on those videos were then downloaded via the YouTube Data API: 2,449,176 comments and 905,869 replies (English only). Classification: a BERT supervised classifier trained on 11,771 labelled COVID-19 social-media posts (4,798 misinformation) drawn from Patwa et al. (2021), whose labels come from fact-checking sites, plus Serrano et al. (2020) conspiratorial YouTube comments; 90/10 train/test split; test accuracy 0.91, fake-class precision 0.93 / recall 0.86 / F1 0.89. No human validation of the classifier on the study corpus itself, no bot filtering, no response rate applicable. Authors flag as limitations the dated training data, the absence of bot/human separation, the English-only scope and the four-channel selection.
rob.item6_quote: We then classified the comments into one of the two following categories by applying a supervised Natural Language Processing classifier: (1) fake: comments that contain claims and speculation which are verifiably not true; and (2) legitimate: comments that do not fall into the fake category.
rob.item10_quote: Overall, the classifier categorized about 21% of the comments and 15% of the replies as fake.
